citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset S^3$ be a compact smooth three-manifold with smooth boundary and let a finite disjoint family of smooth rank-two embedded disks be proper in the following broad sense: each disk has its boundary in $\partial U$ and its interior in $\operatorname{Int}U$. No transversality at its boundary is required. Suppose the topological cut components are three-balls. Then the disks can be replaced by arbitrarily $C^1$-close neat compression disks with exactly the SAME boundary curves, unchanged outside arbitrarily small boundary collars. The new topological cut components correspond to the old ones. After ordinary finite smooth corner rounding the new components are smoothly parametrized standard balls, with labelled disk faces and compatible product collars. Reattaching the disk neighborhoods recovers the actual $U$ and the new disks as their cocores.

The replacement can be supported away from any fixed compact set disjoint from the disk boundary collars, in particular the actual knot arcs and any supplied simultaneous bridge witnesses disjoint from the disks. These objects, their endpoints, ordered pairing and face avoidance are retained. Only the auxiliary compression witnesses change; the surface, attaching curves and actual knot stay fixed. The transport across the initial tangency is a boundary-fixing homeomorphism, smooth separately off its tangency edges; a smooth ambient boundary-preserving diffeomorphism changing tangency is not claimed. The smooth standard-ball assertion uses the full smooth three-dimensional Schoenflies theorem under Countable Choice, rather than a general topological smoothing theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. For $a=0,1$ let
$$P_a=D_{a,0}\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^r\operatorname{int}D_{a,i}\subset\mathbb R^2,$$
where every $D_{a,i}$ is the closed bounded region of a smooth embedded circle, the inner disks are pairwise disjoint, and each lies in the interior of the outer disk $D_{a,0}$. The number $r$ is finite and may be zero. Give $P_a$ the plane orientation. After any chosen labeling of the inner boundary components, let $b_i:\partial D_{0,i}\to\partial D_{1,i}$ be smooth diffeomorphisms all preserving their induced boundary orientations, or all reversing them, $0\le i\le r$.

There is a smooth diffeomorphism $B:P_0\to P_1$ extending all $b_i$, preserving orientation in the first case and reversing it in the second. Moreover, for any specified inward smooth collars $c_{a,i}$ of these boundary components into $P_a$, it may satisfy
$$B(c_{0,i}(p,t))=c_{1,i}(b_i(p),t)$$
for every $i$ and all sufficiently small $t\ge0$, with one common smaller collar width. No parametrization of either hole domain or general classification of smooth surfaces is an additional hypothesis or an imported conclusion.

Let $P$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary, let $N$ be a boundaryless Hausdorff smooth manifold, and let $i:P\to N$ be a smooth embedding. Let $Z\subset N$ be a closed embedded smooth submanifold without boundary. If $i$ is transverse to $Z$ along $\partial P$, then an arbitrarily small jointly smooth ambient isotopy, supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $i(P)$ and fixed on a neighborhood of $i(\partial P)$, makes $i(P)$ transverse to $Z$. The isotopy may be stationary near its time endpoints. No choice axiom is assumed. The same assertion holds for any finite family of such $Z$, provided the initial boundary restriction is transverse to every member. Empty source and empty intersection are allowed.

derivations.claim: Prepare either complete disk system by [F1], without changing its boundary. Its one cut ball has a parametrized sphere boundary with two collared disk faces for each attaching circle. Send that punctured sphere by [F2] to a sphere with paired round holes, one pair inside each of finitely many disjoint round cluster disks. Prescribe the map on one rim of each pair arbitrarily with the required orientation and on the other by composing with its actual original pairing, so the map descends across the signed rim collars. Inside each cluster join its two holes by an embedded arc whose endpoints are paired; in the quotient this gives a smooth simple loop meeting just that attaching circle once. The cluster disks are disjoint, so the loops are pairwise disjoint. The signed collars make their intersections transverse. They can avoid $z$: arrange its image outside the finitely many arcs, or move an arc off that one point by a small local detour. Pull back to obtain dual loops for either system. In particular both attaching systems admit loops crossing their individual circles once and missing all other circles of the SAME system. No condition on intersections with the opposite system has yet been imposed. For genus zero there are no curves, and connectedness of the surface already makes every periodic domain constant; the conclusion is immediate. Assume positive genus from now on. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

Number the original regions and regard real periodic domains with $n_z=0$ as a real subspace $V\subset\mathbb R^r$. It is a rational kernel: subdivide the finite curve graph at its vertices, take the integer matrix sending region coefficients to oriented edge coefficients, require its image to lie in the rational span of full curve vectors, and append $n_z=0$. The coefficients $c_i(P)$ of the alpha circles in $\partial P$ are unique, since full alpha and beta edge vectors have disjoint sets of open edges and each individual circle has an open edge; they are rational linear functions on $V$. The map $c:V\to\mathbb R^g$ is injective. Indeed if its alpha part is zero, $\partial P=\sum_i b_i\beta_i$. Follow the beta-dual loop for $\beta_i$ from step1.1, perturbed to avoid all finite alpha-beta vertices and to cross other curve edges transversely. Across an alpha edge the coefficient jump is zero, and across its sole beta crossing it is $\pm b_i$. The total jump around a closed loop is zero, so $b_i=0$. Thus all boundary jumps vanish. A path on the connected surface joining two region interiors can avoid the finite vertices and cross edges transversely by finitely many small chart detours. It propagates coefficient equality through all regions. Therefore $P$ is constant, and $n_z=0$ makes $P=0$. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

Choose the alpha-dual loops $\gamma_i$ from step1.1 transverse to beta by [F3], keeping them disjoint, avoiding $z$ and retaining their single alpha crossings by making the perturbation small. Choose for each two disjoint parallel copies $\gamma_i^+,\gamma_i^-$, and mutually disjoint annular neighborhoods of all $2g$ copies, avoiding $z$. They meet only $\alpha_i$, in one radial arc. Actual smooth coordinates $(r,\theta)\in(-a,a)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ on each annulus can be chosen with that arc $\theta=0$, by transporting its intersection point around a thin curve collar. Choose $w_i^\pm=(0,\theta_i^\pm)$ with $0<\theta_i^\pm<1$ off beta; there are such points since the central circle is transverse to beta in finitely many points. These points lie off the original curves too. Their region evaluations $n_{w_i^\pm}:V\to\mathbb R$ are rational linear functions. Rational Gaussian elimination and injectivity in step2.1 express each as $\sum_j L_{ij}^\pm c_j(P)$: restrict $c$ to a rational basis of $V$, invert a nonzero maximal minor and extend the resulting left inverse to $\mathbb R^g$. Consequently one finite $C\ge0$ satisfies $|n_{w_i^\pm}(P)|\le C\max_j|c_j(P)|$ for all $P\in V$. If $V=0$ no winding is needed. Otherwise choose an integer $N>C+1$. All this is finite-dimensional linear algebra, with no selection of a basis of an infinite-dimensional space. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Fix a smooth bump $h(r)$ supported in $(-a,a)$, equal to one near $r=0$, and with $0\le h\le1$. On each plus annulus use the isotopy $H_\tau(r,\theta)=(r,\theta-N\tau h(r))$; on each minus annulus use $(r,\theta+N\tau h(r))$, $0\le\tau\le1$. It is the identity near the annulus boundary and is a diffeomorphism for every $\tau$, with inverse obtained by reversing its angular shift. In particular this is an isotopy of the original circles, not a Dehn twist changing their isotopy classes. The supports are disjoint and meet only their prescribed alpha circle, so the operations can be performed one at a time. Orient the radial arc by increasing $r$ first. Its oriented trace has domain coordinates $(\tau,r)$, boundary the final arc minus the initial arc. At a plus testpoint its preimages solve $-N\tau=\theta_i^+\pmod1$ and there are EXACTLY $N$ solutions in $0<\tau<1$. The Jacobian to $(r,\theta)$ has determinant $+Nh(0)>0$, so each contributes $+1$. On the minus annulus the same computation gives determinant $-Nh(0)<0$ and $N$ preimages. Reversing the arc orientation reverses both trace and the convention for its boundary coefficient. Orient each $\alpha_i$ and its annular coordinate consistently so this calculation gives, for its full trace $T_i$, $$n_{w_i^+}(T_i)=N,\qquad n_{w_i^-}(T_i)=-N.$$ For any point off the two arc banks its multiplicity is explicitly the finite signed count of solutions of $\mp N	au h(r)=	heta\pmod1$; this count is locally constant off those banks and its jumps are the stated boundary. Thus the trace chain is defined even if an intermediate circle is tangent to beta. The trace is zero near $z$. This is a computation of an oriented two-chain multiplicity, including the full integer number of turns. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Let $\alpha_i'$ be the final circles before the final transversality perturbation. Their trace satisfies $\partial T_i=\alpha_i'-\alpha_i$. For a periodic domain $P\in V$, set $P'=P+\sum_i c_i(P)T_i$. This is an actual integer region chain when $P$ is integral: the trace's integer local degrees are constant away from the old and new alpha arcs; their boundary jumps are exactly the specified trace boundary. The old alpha jumps cancel in the displayed sum. Thus $\partial P'=\sum_i c_i(P)\alpha_i'+\sum_i b_i(P)\beta_i$, and $n_z(P')=0$. Reversing the isotopy gives the inverse chain operation, so ALL normalized periodic domains of the new system occur this way, with the same full-circle coefficients. At the selected points the supports are disjoint, hence $$n_{w_i^\pm}(P')=n_{w_i^\pm}(P)\pm Nc_i(P).$$ If $P\ne0$, pick an index with $|c_i(P)|=\max_j|c_j(P)|>0$. Step3.1 bounds the two old coefficients by $C|c_i(P)|$, strictly less than $N|c_i(P)|$. Thus these two new coefficients have opposite signs. This works for EVERY real nonzero periodic domain and therefore for every integral one, with one single finite $N$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

The winding may leave tangencies to beta. The final circles miss the finitely many selected testpoints: on the center of each annulus $h=1$ and $N$ is integral, so their intersection there is still at $\theta=0$. Choose small closed testpoint neighborhoods missing all final alpha circles and $z$. Apply [F3] successively to each alpha circle, with arbitrarily small supports excluding those neighborhoods and $z$ and disjoint from all other alpha circles. Compact separation retains disjointness and previous transverse intersections. These final small isotopy traces have zero multiplicity at every testpoint and at $z$, so the inverse-trace bijection of step5.1 preserves its exact sign witnesses. Opposite systems are now transverse, and their intersections are finite by compactness and local transversality. Each surface isotopy of an alpha circle extends over its handlebody by a thin boundary collar: if $K_\tau$ is its supported surface ambient isotopy, the collar map $(p,r)\mapsto(K_{\chi(r)}p,r)$ is a diffeomorphism, identity near its inner boundary, with slice-wise inverse and a triangular derivative. Transport its complete disk system by this map. Thus the manifold and splitting did not change, and the resulting alpha curves still bound a complete system. The basepoint and beta curves never moved. Genus zero and $V=0$ were already included. The claimed global admissibility follows, without a Spin-c, analytic count or move-invariance inference. [F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 treats V=0 by making no winding.
Step 1.1 treats genus zero and step 2.1 excludes the zero normalized domain from the mixed-sign requirement.
Steps 1.1 and 4.1 work for a single attaching circle and its two parallel dual annuli.
Step 1.1 prepares broad auxiliary compression tangencies; step 6.1 removes final opposite-system tangencies without losing sign witnesses.
Step 6.1 fixes z and preserves the actual complete disk-system endpoints of the isotopy.
Steps 2.1 through 6.1 use finite rational elimination, one N and finite supported perturbations.

boundaries.reason: This is an existence theorem, not a characterization.
It does not infer original admissibility from existence of the final diagram.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset S^3$ be a compact smooth three-manifold with smooth boundary and let a finite disjoint family of smooth rank-two embedded disks be proper in the following broad sense: each disk has its boundary in $\partial U$ and its interior in $\operatorname{Int}U$. No transversality at its boundary is required. Suppose the topological cut components are three-balls. Then the disks can be replaced by arbitrarily $C^1$-close neat compression disks with exactly the SAME boundary curves, unchanged outside arbitrarily small boundary collars. The new topological cut components correspond to the old ones. After ordinary finite smooth corner rounding the new components are smoothly parametrized standard balls, with labelled disk faces and compatible product collars. Reattaching the disk neighborhoods recovers the actual $U$ and the new disks as their cocores.

The replacement can be supported away from any fixed compact set disjoint from the disk boundary collars, in particular the actual knot arcs and any supplied simultaneous bridge witnesses disjoint from the disks. These objects, their endpoints, ordered pairing and face avoidance are retained. Only the auxiliary compression witnesses change; the surface, attaching curves and actual knot stay fixed. The transport across the initial tangency is a boundary-fixing homeomorphism, smooth separately off its tangency edges; a smooth ambient boundary-preserving diffeomorphism changing tangency is not claimed. The smooth standard-ball assertion uses the full smooth three-dimensional Schoenflies theorem under Countable Choice, rather than a general topological smoothing theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U$ be a connected oriented smooth handlebody with boundary $\Sigma$. Supply $m$ pairwise disjoint smooth compression disks NEAT at their boundary, actual compatible disk-face collars, and compatible roundings of the cut corners. Suppose cutting along them gives $k\ge1$ parametrized smooth balls. Put $h=m-k+1$, and suppose $h\ge0$.

These finite data construct an orientation-compatible finite polygon presentation of the ACTUAL surface $\Sigma$, with word $\prod_{i=1}^h A_iB_iA_i^{-1}B_i^{-1}$ when $h>0$, and the standard finite sphere presentation when $h=0$. The construction gives the quotient map and finite subdivision into smooth face pieces, rather than inferring their existence from an abstract surface classification. In particular these are the actual finite polygon data required by the diagonal-degree and multipointed sphere-index suppliers.

The construction allows all pairs of faces of the cut balls, including loop pairs on the same ball. It does not require any knot arcs and does not change $\Sigma$ or its orientation. Neat disks, parametrized cut balls and their compatible face collars are hypotheses: no auxiliary tangential disk normalization or identification of a raw cusp cut with a smooth corner is asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.

Fix an admissible multipointed Heegaard diagram with finitely many complementary regions. Fix generators $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ and a vector $a\in\mathbb Z^k$. There are only finitely many nonnegative integral domains of Whitney disks from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$ whose $w$-multiplicity vector is $a$.

More generally, the same conclusion holds for any collection of nonnegative integral region chains whose pairwise differences are periodic domains and whose $w$-multiplicity vector is fixed. If an integer $s$ is prescribed instead of the vector, there are only finitely many such chains with $\sum_i n_{w_i}=s$. In particular this applies to a fixed-index collection whenever an independently established relative grading identity determines that sum from the endpoints and the index. This is finiteness of domains; it makes no assertion about the number of disk classes with a given domain or the compactness of a moduli space.

Assume Countable Choice. Give any actual complete singly pointed Heegaard diagram of a closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold $Y$ as in [[def-hat-heegaard-floer-complex-of-a-closed-three-manifold]], with transverse attaching systems and basepoint $z$. There is a finite sequence of smooth isotopies of individual alpha circles, avoiding $z$ and the other alpha circles, after which opposite systems are again transverse and EVERY nonzero integral periodic region domain with $n_z=0$ has both positive and negative coefficients. The same splitting surface, manifold, basepoint and beta system are retained; the alpha system still bounds a complete compression-disk system.

Thus globally weakly admissible diagrams can be chosen for every such complete splitting, for general $Y$. Neither a rational homology sphere nor a torsion Spin-c premise is imposed. This is the stronger auxiliary global condition, not an assertion that the original diagram already satisfies it or that all admissible inputs must satisfy it. No count invariance along the isotopies, sector-index theorem, strong Spin-c admissibility or Floer move map is asserted.

Assume countable choice. Retain the compact target, totally real boundary submanifolds, fixed path $J_t$ and exact product generator charts of the smooth relative-homotopy index lemma. A continuous Whitney representative from $x$ to $y$ is a continuous disk map with two specified boundary points mapped to $x,y$ and its two boundary arcs mapped into $L_0,L_1$. Equivalence means an actual continuous relative homotopy fixing those points and preserving the two boundary conditions.

Every such class has a smooth fixed-end strip representative, constant on full tails. If two smooth fixed-end representatives are continuously relatively homotopic, there is a smooth relative homotopy between them with one common pair of constant tails and the same fixed endpoints. Consequently the quotient of smooth fixed-end representatives by those smooth homotopies identifies with the continuous Whitney-class set. The actual real Fredholm index of its fixed-end Cauchy–Riemann-symbol linearization therefore defines an integer $\mu(\phi)$ on every continuous Whitney class; it agrees with the actual index of each smooth fixed-end model, is additive under class concatenation, is zero on the constant class, and changes sign under reversal.

For an actual smooth finite-energy holomorphic strip with uniform generator ends, its actual Fredholm index equals this index of its continuously compactified Whitney class.

This proves a continuous-class index using genuine representatives and relative homotopies. It does not identify that integer with a domain Euler measure, corner multiplicities or a first-Chern pairing; no nonlinear moduli counts or their regularity are asserted.

Assume countable choice. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold with a smooth path $J_t$ of almost complex structures, and let $L_0,L_1$ be compact submanifolds totally real for $J_0,J_1$, respectively. Suppose their intersection is finite and transverse. At each intersection point choose a target chart in which $L_0=\mathbb R^m$, $L_1=i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t=i$ for every $t$. Retain those same charts and structures throughout.

A smooth fixed-end representative from $x$ to $y$ is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ with boundary on $L_0,L_1$, identically $x$ on one full negative tail and identically $y$ on one full positive tail. Its covariant Cauchy–Riemann linearization on fixed-end $H^1\to L^2$ spaces is Fredholm. Its real index is independent of the chosen smooth connection and of the representative under any smooth relative homotopy $H(h,s,t)$ with those boundary conditions, fixed endpoints, and one common pair of constant tails for all $h\in[0,1]$.

These indices add under concatenating two such representatives at their common endpoint, are zero for a constant representative, and change sign when $u(s,t)$ is replaced by $u(-s,t)$. Thus they define an integer index on smooth fixed-end representatives modulo the stated smooth relative homotopies, with concatenation and reversal laws. This result includes nonholomorphic representatives. It does not assume that a nonlinear moduli space exists or is regular.

A further relative smoothing and end-flattening argument is required to identify this smooth quotient with a Whitney-class set defined initially by arbitrary continuous disk maps and continuous relative homotopies. No such identification, domain Euler formula, or arbitrary-class representativity theorem is asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface, $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ with its standard complex structure, and $m\ge1$. For $a\in\Sigma$ put $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. This is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at repeated tuples. The universal incidence hypersurface $\mathcal E=\{(a,D):D\in E_a\}\subset\Sigma\times X$ carries a smooth complex divisor line bundle with its canonical section, whose zero set is $\mathcal E$ with multiplicity one.

For a smooth map $v:S\to X$, where $S$ is an oriented sphere or a closed disk, define $n_a(v)$ as the degree of the pullback point-divisor line bundle; for a disk use the canonical section to trivialize it on the boundary, and require $v(\partial S)\cap E_a=\varnothing$. The proof constructs this integer by elementary frame winding. It is defined even when a sphere lies wholly in $E_a$.

For a sphere, $n_a(v)$ is independent of $a$ on all of $\Sigma$. For a disk whose boundary tuples have all entries in a finite union of curves $\Gamma\subset\Sigma$, it is independent of $a$ on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$. If $v^{-1}(E_a)$ is finite and the map is holomorphic on a neighborhood of every one of these points, then
$$n_a(v)=\sum_{z\in v^{-1}(E_a)}\operatorname{ord}_z(F_a\circ v)\ge0,$$
where $F_a$ is any local holomorphic defining function of the smooth hypersurface $E_a$. Each term is a positive integer. Thus the degree agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity, while divisor containment is handled by its degree definition and actual point movement rather than an unsupported proper-intersection assumption.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented Riemann surface with an actual finite oriented polygon as in the sphere-index theorem, $m\ge1$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$. Let $\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta$ be two disjoint-within-system smooth curve families of size $m$, transverse to each other, with product tori $L_\alpha,L_\beta$. Give two smooth fixed-end Whitney disk models $u,v$ from the same generator $x$ to the same generator $y$, constant near their two marked boundary corners, with their actual fixed product end data. Use the auxiliary complex-structure homotopies and actual relative-index realizations specified in the relative Whitney index theorem. Domain coefficients mean the integer relative degrees of the point-divisor lines, not a holomorphic representative assumption.

For any such pair, $D(u)-D(v)$ has boundary a sum of full attaching circles. The coefficient on each oriented circle is the angular winding difference of the corresponding labelled boundary paths, with their source-boundary signs. In particular, if $D(u)=D(v)$ as region chains, their boundary paths on each labelled alpha circle are homotopic relative their endpoints, and likewise on each labelled beta circle. After these boundary homotopies the difference of their smooth relative classes is represented by a sphere $A$ with $n_z(A)=0$. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(u)=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(v),$$
before source translation, on all the stated higher Sobolev and allowed smooth weighted realizations. Thus actual Fredholm index is well defined on the set of REALIZED Whitney domains, including classes with positive, zero or negative marked multiplicities. No assertion that every integer region chain is realized is made.

The analogous statement holds for two smooth disks based at the same point of a single product torus $L_\gamma$, with equal one-system domains: their boundary loops are based homotopic, and their boundary Maslov indices and compact-disk Fredholm indices agree. Their fixed-node indices also agree whenever that bounded point-trace realization is used. The finite polygon hypothesis is supplied for the original embedded balanced $S^3$ data by the broad-input application in the sphere-index theorem. No full formula $e(D)+n_x(D)+n_y(D)$, normalized relative or absolute grading, invariance, or arbitrary-domain representativity is included.

Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface, $m\ge1$, and $p\in\Sigma$. In the complex symmetric product $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ let $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. Let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact submanifolds disjoint from $E_p$. Suppose $J_t$ agrees with the fixed complex structure of $X$ on one neighborhood of $E_p$ for every $t\in[0,1]$. Let $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ be a smooth solution of $\partial_\tau u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with boundary on $L_0,L_1$ and uniform limits as $\tau\to\pm\infty$ at points of $L_0\cap L_1$.

The intersections of $u$ with $E_p$ are a finite collection of interior points, each with positive integral local intersection multiplicity. Their sum is nonnegative, and it is zero exactly when $u$ avoids $E_p$. In pointed Heegaard data, with $L_0,L_1$ the product tori and $p$ any marked point, this proves nonnegativity of the domain multiplicity $n_p(u)$ whenever it is defined by intersection with $E_p$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(\Sigma,j)$ be a closed Riemann surface with positive area form $\eta$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$, $m\ge1$, with its induced complex structure $J_0$. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient, $\Delta\subset X$ its repeated-point locus, and $\Omega=\sum_{l=1}^m\operatorname{pr}_l^*\eta$. Off $\Delta$ the permutation-invariant form $\Omega$ descends to a smooth form $\omega$ on $X\setminus\Delta$. Equip $X$ with any smooth Riemannian metric $g$.

Let $L_\alpha,L_\beta$ be product tori formed from two finite systems of pairwise disjoint attaching curves, with transverse intersections between the systems. Suppose a smooth path $J_t$ agrees with $J_0$ on a neighborhood $V$ of $\Delta$ and tames $\omega$ on $X\setminus V$. Let $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ be a smooth $J_t$-holomorphic strip, with boundary on these tori, finite $g$-Dirichlet energy, and uniform limits at both ends to intersection generators. For each complementary region $R$ of the attaching curves write $n_R(u)$ for the signed intersection multiplicity of $u$ with $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ at a generic $p\in R$.

There is a constant $C$ depending only on the fixed geometric data and the path, independent of $u$, such that
$$E_g(u)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R\times[0,1]}(|u_s|_g^2+|u_t|_g^2)\,dsdt\le C\sum_R n_R(u)\int_R\eta.$$
In particular energies of all such representatives with one fixed domain are uniformly bounded. The finite-energy hypothesis here is explicit; no assertion that arbitrary asymptotically convergent smooth solutions automatically have finite energy is included.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix compact transverse strip data with finite generator set $K=L_0\cap L_1$, and a smooth background path $J_t^b$ constant on endpoint collars, with fixed totally real boundary structures and exact all-$t$ charts taking the two boundaries to $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t^b$ to $i$. Choose pairwise disjoint compact neighborhoods $A_x$ of the generators inside those charts and a compact set $D$ disjoint from their union. Choose smaller working generator charts with closures inside $\operatorname{Int}(A_x)$. All references to preserved exact generator charts below mean these smaller working charts; the original larger background charts remain available to analyze a strip whose entire image lies in $A_x$. Put $P_X=D\cup\bigcup_xA_x$, and require all desired spatially protected values on $P_X$. For an optional tameness requirement, assume the closure of $X\setminus P_X$ is a compact subset of an open region carrying the specified smooth two-form and that $J^b$ tames that form there.

There is an actual separable Hilbert ball of smooth paths $J_t(a)$ preserving the protected spatial values, generator charts, boundary structures and optional tameness, such that every derivative of $J(a)-J^b$ at $t=0,1$ vanishes. Finite parameter tangent combinations are dense in every finite coefficient norm in the smooth anti-$J(a)$ fields compactly supported in $(0,1)\times(X\setminus P_X)$. The actual universal strip section is a submersion at every nonconstant finite-energy strip, including those with the same end generator. A dense residual set of parameters makes all these actual strip linearizations surjective in $H^1\to L^2$ and in every integer higher Hilbert Sobolev realization simultaneously.

These auxiliary paths are not asserted to be constant on any endpoint collar. Every one is, however, a smooth coefficient limit of paths $J^{(\epsilon)}$ which are constant on genuine endpoint collars, have the same protected spatial and boundary values and exact generator charts, and retain tameness. No regularity of those approximating paths is asserted here. Transferring regularity to them requires a separate compactness and operator argument; a limit of shrinking collars is not treated as an admissible fixed-collar path.

Assume Countable Choice and the nearly symmetric marked strip geometry of the zero-marked bubble-exclusion lemma. In particular all individual boundary curve-system complement components contain marked points, and the almost complex paths have common exact product generator charts, common protected diagonal/region/marked-divisor neighborhoods, and fixed totally real boundary structures. Let $J^*$ be a smooth path in this geometry such that every nonconstant finite-energy zero-marked $J^*$ strip has surjective actual $H^1\to L^2$ linearization. It need not be constant on time-endpoint collars. Fix $E_0<\infty$.

Suppose $J_n\to J^*$ smoothly, with those same fixed geometric structures, including the common generator charts, and uniform nearly symmetric energy constants. Then for all sufficiently large $n$, every zero-marked $J_n$ strip of energy at most $E_0$ has surjective actual linearization. In fact specified right inverses $L^2\to H^1$ can be chosen with one uniform finite bound for all these strips and all sufficiently large $n$, using a fixed smooth target connection flat in the generator charts. Surjectivity also holds in every integer higher Hilbert Sobolev realization.

Consequently a generic auxiliary flat-endpoint-jet path supplied by the flat-jet universal regularity theorem has genuine constant-collar approximating paths which are regular for all zero-marked strips of energy at most this fixed $E_0$. This supplies bounded-energy constant-collar regularity, including same-generator strips. It does not supply a uniform energy bound for all Floer classes of a prescribed index; any such admissibility/domain-index argument remains a separate prerequisite for unrestricted moduli counts or index-two compactifications.

Assume Countable Choice and the complete marked nearly symmetric geometry, protected neighborhoods and exact product generator charts of the zero-marked bubble-exclusion lemma. Fix $E_0<\infty$, end generators $x_-,x_+$, and an actual smooth path $J_t$ for which every nonconstant zero-marked strip of energy at most $E_0$ has surjective actual linearization. Such a path with genuine endpoint collars is supplied by the bounded-energy collar-openness lemma.

There are finitely many longitudinal-translation orbits of nonconstant zero-marked $J_t$ strips from $x_-$ to $x_+$ with energy at most $E_0$ and real Fredholm index one. This remains true simultaneously over the finite set of ordered end pairs. Their counts modulo two are therefore well-defined integers modulo two. The index is the actual $H^1\to L^2$ operator index, before translation quotient. No identification with a separately named Maslov or domain index is asserted, and the theorem supplies no energy bound for an unrestricted collection of Floer classes.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix the compact nearly symmetric Heegaard geometry with complete marked cut systems, protected diagonal and region-divisor neighborhoods, and common exact product generator charts used in zero-marked bubble exclusion. Every complement component of each individual boundary curve system must contain a marked point. Whitney classes mean continuous two-marked disk relative-homotopy classes with the two boundary arcs on the specified product tori. Their integer $\mu$ is the actual fixed-end Fredholm index constructed by continuous relative smoothing, not a domain Euler formula.

Fix a class $\phi:x\to z$ with $\mu(\phi)=2$ and with all marked divisor degrees zero. Its region divisor degrees $n_R(\phi)$ are well-defined integers. For a common domain-energy constant $C$ put
$$B_\phi=C\sum_R|n_R(\phi)|\int_R\eta.$$
Choose a smooth path with genuine constant endpoint collars, the stipulated protected data, and actual regularity for every nonconstant zero-marked strip of energy at most a number $E_0>B_\phi$. Such paths exist by the auxiliary flat-jet regularity and actual bounded-energy collar-approximation theorems, with $C$ taken uniform in the approximating neighborhood as proved below.

For this path, the moduli space $\widehat{\mathcal M}(\phi)$ of actual strips in $\phi$ modulo longitudinal translation is a Hausdorff second-countable topological one-manifold. It has a compactification by finitely many boundary points. These points are exactly the ordered pairs of actual index-one strip orbits
$$([u],[v]),\qquad u:x\to y,\quad v:y\to z,\quad [u]*[v]=\phi.$$
Each such component has zero marked degrees and energy at most $B_\phi$. Each boundary point has the actual one-sided gluing collar with smooth interior from the regular-pair collar theorem. No differentiability at a prescribed compactifying parameter is asserted.

The number of these boundary points is even. Equivalently the sum modulo two of the products of rigid counts over the factorizations $\phi=\phi_1*\phi_2$ with $\mu(\phi_1)=\mu(\phi_2)=1$ is zero; only finitely many factors with nonzero counts occur. This is the cancellation identity for this fixed zero-marked class. It does not establish finiteness over all classes of prescribed index, a domain-index formula, positive-marked boundary-degeneration cancellation, or polygon/target-degeneration gluing.

derivations.claim: If the genus is zero, the target is a point and the stated one-generator zero differential follows directly; assume henceforth positive genus. Prepare the geometric data without a category narrowing. View either actual handlebody as an abstract regular neighborhood of its finite graph, transport it to the standard ball-with-handles model embedded in $S^3$, apply [F1]'s broad same-boundary compression preparation there and transport back. The surface, attaching circles and diagram in $Y$ are unchanged. The resulting one-ball cut supplies the actual finite polygon needed by [F3]. To choose genuine integrable crossing charts, at each of finitely many crossings take a positive smooth chart $\Psi$ straightening the two arcs and an old holomorphic chart $c$. The positive local germ $c^{-1}\Psi$ fixes that crossing. Extend it by [F1] to a diffeomorphism supported in a small crossing disk, identity near its boundary. Choose these disks disjoint and off all chosen region points and $z$. Their finite composite $F$ gives the actual integrable structure $j=F^*j_{\mathrm{ref}}$; the charts $cF=\Psi$ are holomorphic, with unchanged holomorphic transition maps. Their products give common $\mathbb R^h/i\mathbb R^h$ generator charts in $\operatorname{Sym}^h\Sigma$. Choose protected diagonal and region-divisor neighborhoods separated from the two compact tori and smaller generator charts, and use the constant standard background path. No interpolation of surface complex structures has been presumed integrable. [F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

Prove domain finiteness independently of an index bound and BEFORE choosing regular counts. Number the regions and let $L\subset\mathbb R^r$ consist of real periodic chains with $n_z=0$. The finite integer boundary matrix, modulo the full-circle span, makes $L$ a rational linear kernel. It contains no nonzero nonnegative vector: if $v\ge0$ were nonzero, restrict to the face of its strictly positive coordinates. A rational basis of that restricted kernel and sufficiently close rational approximations to the finitely many coefficients of $v$ give a nonzero rational nonnegative vector. Clearing denominators contradicts the assumed integral mixed-sign condition. Fix endpoints $x,y$ and collect the nonnegative domains of ALL continuous zero-basepoint Whitney classes between them. If the collection is nonempty, choose one domain $D_0$. Differences have their endpoint corners cancel by [F3], so the collection lies in $(D_0+L)\cap\mathbb R^r_{\ge0}$. Its integral members are bounded: otherwise choose, using a fixed enumeration of $\mathbb Z^r$, integral members of norm exceeding each integer. Normalize them. A subsequence has a nonnegative unit-vector limit, by successive subdivision of the finite coordinate cube and retention of the first subcube containing infinitely many indices. Its difference from $D_0/\|D_n\|$ lies in the closed kernel $L$, so the limit is a forbidden nonzero nonnegative member of $L$. Thus there are only finitely many integral domains for this pair. This is the actual [F2] argument, requiring no rational-homology-sphere premise. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Take the finite union $\mathcal D$ of these finite sets over the finite generator pairs. Let $C$ be a common domain-energy constant on the small protected coefficient family in [F4] and put $$B=\max\left(\{C\sum_R n_R(D)\int_R\eta:D\in\mathcal D\}\cup\{0\}\right),\qquad E_*=B+1.$$ Every actual zero-basepoint holomorphic strip has a nonnegative region domain, by protected-divisor positivity, hence has energy at most $B$ by [F4]. More importantly, any concatenation of two such strips has a nonnegative domain, zero basepoint degree and a continuous Whitney class by [F3]; its domain is itself in $\mathcal D$. Its fixed-class bound $B_\phi=C\sum_R|n_R(\phi)|\int_R\eta$ is therefore at most $B$ too. This uniform bound uses all continuous nonnegative domains, not just eventually counted strips. There is no claim that two classes with the same domain are equal, or that all signed domains are bounded. [F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Use the zero-mark set consisting ONLY of $z$; the additional protected region divisors are not required to have zero degree. Choose in this protected family an auxiliary all-strip regular flat-jet path from [F4]. Its genuine constant-collar approximants have the same surface, boundary structures, generator charts and common energy constant. The bounded-energy zero-marked openness theorem in [F4] makes every sufficiently late approximant regular on every nonconstant zero-basepoint strip of energy at most $E_*$. Fix one. Step 3.1 bounds ALL of its actual zero-basepoint strips by $B<E_*$, so it is regular for all of them, including every possible limiting level; no negative-index nonregular level is left uncontrolled. This also implies each nonconstant such strip has positive actual index, since its nonzero longitudinal derivative is a square-integrable kernel section by its exact end decay and onto-ness. Applying the actual finite-count assertion in [F5] now gives finitely many index-one orbits across every generator pair and represented class. Their modulo-two finite sums define a matrix on the finite vector space. [F4, F5, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Fix initial and final generators. A term in the coefficient of their differential square is an ordered pair of these finitely many rigid orbits. Its concatenated continuous class $\phi$ has zero basepoint degree and actual index two by [F3]. There are only finitely many such ordered pairs and hence finitely many such concatenated classes; distinct classes with identical domains are not identified. For EACH of these actual classes step 3.1 gives $B_\phi\le B<E_*$. The chosen path is regular on its entire required zero-basepoint energy range by step 4.1, so [F5]'s fixed-class compactification and parity theorem apply. Its boundary pairs are exactly all the rigid orbit pairs whose concatenated class is this $\phi$. Their number is even. Summing this identity over the finite list of actual concatenated classes exhausts the coefficient of the differential square and makes it zero in $\mathbb F_2$. No summation over merely formal domains, no finiteness assumption for arbitrary class sets, and no positive-mark boundary-degeneration theorem were used. [F3, F5, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

If the supplied complete splitting is not globally weakly admissible, first apply [F2]'s winding theorem. It leaves $Y$, the splitting surface and basepoint fixed, retains complete disk systems and ends with transverse curves satisfying exactly the global hypothesis used in step 2.1. The preceding construction applies to that diagram. No chain map comparing its counts to counts on the original diagram has been supplied by the winding theorem or by this proof. In particular the conclusion is existence of an actual finite chosen-data complex for general closed $Y$, not its topological invariance, a construction for every weaker sector-admissible input, or a grading assertion. Genus zero was settled in step 1.1; the empty-set cases in steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $B=0$ and a finite zero module if no positive-genus generators exist.
